text:
Someone wants to know how to say "the dessert is ready, come and eat" in another language.
Translate that into Spanish
how do you say it in French
Give me two or three ways to say it in Italian
What is the German for "come and eat"?
Can you say it in Portuguese, but only half as formal?
I need a nicer, more polite way to say this in Japanese, please
Could you help me tell my grandmother in Polish that the sweet things are waiting? I want to say it right, and a bit longer than just one word.

Abena woke up and her head felt heavy. She rubbed her eyes, picked up her phone and said, "Plan our dinners for this week and make me a shopping list." The assistant asked if anyone in the house had a diet. "No pork, and not too much salt," said Abena. In a moment the screen showed seven dinners, from lentil soup on Monday to fish and rice on Sunday. None of them had pork. Below the menu was a shopping list, sorted by the aisles of her shop. The assistant said the soup would take about one hour to cook, and that it might sound plain but would taste great. Abena smiled. The list looked smooth and tidy, with nothing repeated. She sipped her tea, saved the plan, and asked the assistant to send it to her husband too. It did, and he sent back a thumbs up before she had finished breakfast.

Someone wants a bike route home from their yoga class that is not dark or lonely at night.
Bike route home, lit please
Show me a safe way to ride from the studio to my flat
Which streets have lights for cycling at night?
Give me the name of a cycle path that stays bright after sunset
I would rather not ride through the park in the evening, is there another way?
Find me a route on main roads, I don't like cycling when it's late
Could you please plan a ride home with street lights all the way? My class ends at nine and I get nervous riding alone after sunset.

Femke stood at the front door with a lunchbox in one hand and a school bag in the other. "Remind me to collect my parcel at the post office," she told her phone, "and please don't remind me before four, because I am in meetings until then." The assistant set a reminder for a quarter past four. Femke thought for a second. "I don't want the big post office by the market. The small one on Elm Street is closer." The assistant changed the place on the reminder and showed her the opening hours. Closing time was six. When she came home with the box under her arm, she said, "Mark that as done." The assistant crossed it off her list and asked if she needed anything else. "Not today," said Femke, and she went to make dinner.

Nok was stirring a big pot of soup when a guest from Brazil walked into the kitchen. "How do you say welcome in Portuguese, and can you spell it for me?" she asked her phone. The assistant said "bem-vindo" out loud and spelled it letter by letter. Nok wrote it on a card and put it at the front of the menu board. The guest had just won a prize at the food fair, so Nok wanted to learn a few more words. She asked the assistant to show only the words about food, and it filtered the list down to soup, rice, bread and water. Nok practised each one while the soup bubbled. When the guest sat down, she said "bem-vindo" with a big smile, and he laughed and clapped.

A phone's contact list is a small book of people. It is for finding a number or an address fast, so you do not have to remember it. People change their contacts all the time. They say, "Save this number for Dana," or "Change Grandma's address, she moved," or "Put a birthday on my cousin's card." Some people dress up a contact with a photo or a special ringtone, so the phone shows who is calling. On a foggy morning, when your head is slow, it helps that the assistant can find a name for you. You can also say "Delete the old number" or "Put Dana's work phone first." The list stays tidy that way.

Weather forecasts tell us what the sky will do, so we can plan our day. People look at them to decide if they need a coat, an umbrella or sunscreen. A forecast can change, because the wind may shift in the afternoon and bring rain. People ask, "Will it rain today?" or "How cold is it outside?" or "Do I need a jacket tomorrow?" A sailor may check the wind before tying a rope on a boat, and a gardener may check before hanging washing on a line. Many people read the final forecast just before leaving home. If they want another place, they say, "What about Lisbon?" or "Show me the weekend."

At lunch, Lotte sat at her desk and spoke to her phone. "Could you please tell me how much electricity the house used yesterday? I am asking because last month's bill was very high and I want to be careful this time." The assistant checked the meter and said the house had used fourteen units, which was more than normal. It said the dryer and the oven had been on for a long time. Lotte remembered that her brother had said the wire on the old heater felt loose. "Remind me tonight to call an electrician," she said. The assistant set the reminder. It also said the power company would deliver the next bill on Friday, and offered to tell her the total every evening this week. Lotte said yes and went back to her salad.

Olivia sat in her chair at work and looked at a photo of the vegetables she had chopped for the office party. "This picture is so dark. I can't see any of the colors," she said. The assistant made the photo brighter, and now the red peppers and green onions shone. Olivia was glad. She scrolled to another one, where her team was laughing around the table. "My mum would love to see this," she said, half to herself. The assistant asked if it should send the photo to Mum. "Yes, please, just that one, and put it in the party album too." The assistant sent the photo and saved a copy in the album. A minute later Mum sent back three hearts, and Olivia put her phone down with a big smile.

A birthday list is a way to remember who is turning a year older and when. People keep it in a phone so they never forget a date. It is also for gift ideas: you write a tiny note, like "Sam likes tea," and follow it up when the day comes near. People change the list by saying, "Remind me about Mum's birthday a week before," or "Change Sam's gift to a book," or "Save Leo's phone number so I can text him." Some even ask, "What number birthday is Dad having?" When the date is close, the assistant tells them what is on the list, and they can say, "Buy that one" or "Show me cheaper ideas."

name: print_copies
does: Prints several copies of a document, like a flyer for a salty snack sale or a notice about a snow day, so one page is multiplied into a neat stack.
inputs: the document or file name, how many copies, and which printer to use
people say:
- Print ten of these
- I need twenty copies of the snow day letter for tomorrow
- Run off a few more of that flyer
- Make one for everyone in the class, there are thirty of us
- Can you print this again, five times please?
- Give me a stack of the menu for the party

name: book_time_left
does: Tells you how long it will take to finish a book at your usual speed, so you can plan a snowy weekend of reading.
inputs: the book's title, the page you are on, and how many pages you read in an hour; it does not need the weight of the book or how worn the cover is
people say:
- How long until I finish this book?
- Will I be done with my novel by Sunday?
- How many hours of reading are left?
- I'm on page two hundred, how much more do I have?
- Tell me how long chapter nine will take
- Can I get through this before the trip?

Nandi was a little girl with a piggy bank shaped like a frog. One evening, before going to sleep, she spoke to the tablet in her room. "I don't want to buy sweets this month. Can you help me save for a bike?" The assistant asked how much money she had. "Twelve dollars," said Nandi. The assistant said the bike she liked cost forty dollars, so she needed twenty-eight more. It made a plan: put away four dollars each week, and the bike would be hers in seven weeks. Nandi nodded and asked it to switch off the lamp. The assistant did, and then it saved the plan with a little picture of a bike. "Good night," said Nandi, and she hugged her frog bank.

Kwame was at his desk when his video call froze again. He had tried every route he could think of: moving the cable, standing near the window, even shouting at the screen. At last he spoke to his phone. "Restart the router tonight at midnight, please. And tomorrow, switch the guest network off after the meeting at ten." The assistant set both jobs. It also told him that his local provider had reported slow service in his street, which might be the real problem. Kwame sighed. "Then tell me when it is fixed." The assistant said it would check every hour and send him a message. Kwame leaned back, took a sip of tea, and decided to finish the call on his phone for now.

After a good clean with the broom, someone wants the total of the electricity they have used by the end of the week.
Total power used this week?
how many units have we burned so far
What's our electric bill up to now this week?
Add up the electricity from Monday to today
Is my usage so far this week good, or is it high?
Tell me the total by Sunday night, please
Could you please sum up our energy use for the week so far? I'd like to know before the end of the week so I can change what I do.

Measurements tell us how long, how heavy or how hot something is. In a kitchen, a drawer full of cups and spoons helps, but recipes from other countries use different units. People change them by asking, "How many cups is 250 millilitres?" or "What is 350 degrees Fahrenheit in Celsius?" or "How many pounds is two kilos?" Friends share recipes and plans with numbers like these, and a noisy kitchen is no place to do sums in your head. So people ask out loud: "Turn miles into kilometres," "Make that in inches," or "Give me that in grams." The answer helps them follow the recipe or buy the right amount.

Babies sleep and eat on a rhythm, and parents often keep a simple plan for it. A feeding time says when the next bottle is due, and a nap time says when the baby should be in bed. Many families have a baby monitor too, which lets them hear or see the room from far away. Plans change, so people say, "Move the nap to two o'clock," or "Remind me to feed her in an hour," or "Let me know if he wakes up." On Tuesday the plan may be different from Monday, since the baby grows. It helps to have the times correct, so people say, "Show me today's schedule" or "Change the evening feed."

Someone wants the house cooler after the oven has been on and the kids bathe, but doesn't want it freezing.
Cool the kitchen, but not too much
Don't make it freezing, just a bit cooler
Turn the fan on low, I don't want the loud one
It's roasting in here since I used the oven
Cool down the house to twenty-two, not lower
I don't want the air conditioning on all night, but cool the bedroom before bed
Could you cool the living room for about an hour? It's true that I like it fresh, but I don't want the baby to get cold.

Meera looked out of the kitchen window and frowned. The sky was gray. "I wonder if I'll get soaked on the way home," she said to her phone. The assistant checked the weather and said rain would start at seven. Her ride home takes twenty-five minutes, so it suggested she leave at half past six. Meera nodded and opened the route document her cycling club had sent. She tapped the wrong button and the file filled with strange letters. "Oops, undo that," she said. The assistant undid the last change, and the route came back. It showed the short way along the river. Meera wiped her hands on her apron, thanked the assistant, and went back to her pots, glad to know she would stay dry.

A calendar is where we keep the things we plan to do: meetings, classes, trips and time with friends. It is for seeing what is coming and for finding a free hour. People change it all the time. They say, "Move my dentist visit to Friday," "Cancel the meeting at three," or "Make lunch with Ana go an hour longer." Before a hike in the mountain hills, someone might ask, "Am I free on Saturday morning?" A quiet week with nothing in it is easy to see. Many people also say, "Put a reminder before it starts," so they do not forget. It is simple: if you want to go somewhere, put it on the calendar.

Someone wants a quick sum: a yellow kite costs nineteen dollars, the sale takes ten off, and they don't want to blow their money.
nineteen minus ten
What is nineteen take away ten?
19 less 10?
If something costs nineteen and I save ten, what do I pay?
Subtract ten from nineteen
Quick, nineteen minus ten
Could you work out the price of the kite for me? It says nineteen dollars, and there is a discount of ten dollars.

Text messages are short notes we send from a phone. They are for quick things, like "I'm running late" or "Dinner at seven." Group chats let many people talk at once, such as a family or a team. People often ask the assistant to read a message out loud or to write one back. They say, "Text my mother that I am on my way," "Reply yes," or "Tell the group I'll be there at eight." Sometimes they want to change a message: "Make that shorter" or "Say sorry instead." If you have to wake early, you may say, "Send a text to Sam at six." One short reply is enough most of the time.

Olivia had just moved to the city, and tomorrow was her friend Hana's birthday. She did not know the shops yet. "I need a gift for Hana," she told her phone. "I don't want flowers, because she sneezes around them. And I don't want anything big." The assistant asked how much she wanted to spend. "About twenty dollars." It suggested a small plant, a scarf or a book, and then pulled up a map of three shops near her flat. A scarf in a shop window on Maple Street caught her eye. "Is that one open now?" The assistant said it closed at six, and offered to save a note to have the gift ready by five. Olivia said yes and put on her coat.

Music on a phone or speaker is for filling a room with songs you like. People pick a song, an artist or a playlist, and change the volume or skip a track. In the car, music is easy to control by voice, so hands stay on the wheel and a foot stays near the brake. People say, "Play something calm," "Turn it down," "Skip this one," or "Play my morning playlist." The phone may beep when a new message comes in, and then people say, "Pause the music." When a song makes them glad, they ask, "Play that again" or "More songs like this."

name: bin_day_lookup
does: Tells you which bin goes out on which day at your address, so no one has to cry over a smelly missed pickup, whether it is a home or a small hotel.
inputs: the street address and the kind of waste, like paper, glass, food scraps or general rubbish; the answer is fast
people say:
- Which bin goes out tonight?
- When do they take the glass?
- Is tomorrow a compost day?
- Did I miss the rubbish truck this week?
- Does cardboard go in the blue one?
- What do I put out on Thursday?

name: log_baby_nap
does: Writes down when the baby fell asleep and woke up, so parents can understand the sleep pattern, and shows it on the family's website page.
inputs: the time the baby fell asleep, the time the baby woke up, and a note if you like, such as a dark room or a noisy street
people say:
- She just fell asleep, write that down
- He woke up at three
- How long did the baby nap today?
- Keep track of his sleep for me
- Note that the room was too dark and she cried
- Show me this week's naps

In elderly care, small helpers make life easier and safer. A medicine reminder says when to take a pill, and a check-in call lets a family hear that grandma is fine. For an emergency, a button or a word calls for help. People change these things as needs change: "Remind Dad about his pills at eight," "Call my aunt every morning," or "Bring up the number for the doctor." A notebook by the phone helps too, with names and times written in it. The family wants every time to be correct, so they ask, "Read the reminders back to me" and "Change the evening one to nine o'clock."

Podcasts and audiobooks are stories and talks you listen to instead of read. Each podcast has episodes, and each audiobook has chapters. The player remembers where you left off, so you can start again later. People change how they listen: "Play it faster," "Go back thirty seconds," or "Skip to the next chapter." A grandfather may like a slow speed, so he says, "Slow it down a little." Some people swipe the screen to move on, but others just talk and say, "Next episode." Many players are automatic and start the next episode alone. If you do not want that, say, "Stop after this one."

Someone wants the current score of the football match, because their stream keeps freezing and the pizza is in the oven.
Score?
what's the score right now
Who is winning the match?
Has the game started yet? It's meant to kick off before lunch on Sunday
Give me the latest result for my team
Tell me how Sunday's match is going, I'm busy before lunch
Could you please read me the score as soon as anything happens? I'll be cooking before lunch on Sunday and can't watch.

Someone wants to know how many days are left until a nice event, like a garage sale, and may want to reset the count later.
Days until the twelfth of March?
how long till March twelfth
Count down to the twelfth of March for me
How many sleeps until the twelfth of March?
How many weeks are there before the twelfth of March?
I need the number of days between today and the twelfth of March, please
Could you tell me how many days remain until the twelfth of March? I want to plan the garage sale and see how much time I have.

name: parking_time_left
does: Tells you how many minutes are left on your parking ticket and warns you before it ends, so drivers who love a long lunch can come back to no fine.
inputs: the place where you parked, such as the apron in front of the bakery, your ticket time, and the size of your car, small, medium or large
people say:
- How long do I have on my ticket?
- Warn me before my parking runs out
- Am I still okay in this spot?
- Tell me ten minutes before I have to move the car
- I'm at the shops, how much time is left?
- Will I get a fine if I stay till two?

Layla got home after a night shift with sore shoulders and tired eyes. The morning sky was grey. She had an appointment with the physio at noon, and a long soak in the hot tub sounded wonderful. She dropped her bag, looked out at the garden and sighed. "Brr, that water must be cold as a lake. I want to get in before my appointment." The assistant understood. It started the heater on the hot tub and set the water to thirty-eight degrees. "It will be warm in about forty minutes," it said, and offered to tell her when it was ready. Layla made a cup of tea, put on a soft robe, and waited. When the assistant gave its message, she slipped into the warm water with a happy sigh.

Parking is about leaving a car in a safe place while you do something else. People look for a free spot, pay for the time, and watch how much time is left. On a hot day the street can bathe in sun, so many drivers look for shade. Many places let you upload a photo of your ticket or pay with a phone. People change their parking by saying, "Add another hour," "How much time is left?" or "Remind me ten minutes before it ends." A silent phone can be a problem, so a good reminder buzzes. They also ask, "Find a spot near the library" or "Where did I park?"

Delroy sat in heavy traffic with both hands on the wheel. The road was jammed for miles. "Play the next episode of my podcast about old trains," he said to the car. "But don't start from the beginning. I already heard the first half." The assistant found the spot where he had left off and began to play. Delroy let out a breath. At a red light, he tried to stretch his back against the seat. Then he said, "Make it a bit faster. I don't want to be late for the end." The assistant raised the speed a little, and the host's voice sped up. Delroy smiled. The cars did not move, but the story did, and the time passed quickly.

Isaac stood on a ladder in his shop, hanging a new sign above the door, when his phone buzzed. His sister was flying in from Lagos. He climbed down. "Is my sister's flight on time, and can you text her the gate number?" he asked. The assistant checked and said the plane was running late by forty minutes. There had been several delays that morning because of fog. It sent his sister a text with the new gate. Isaac thanked it. "Tell me again when it lands," he said. The assistant promised. Isaac went back up the ladder, finished the sign, and had time to sweep the floor before the customers came.

Notes are small written pieces to keep ideas from slipping away. Maybe it is a shopping list, a thought for work, or a voice note you said out loud. People use notes to find things later, like the cheese you wanted to buy or the number for the plumber. Notes change: "Add eggs to my list," "Find my note about the trip," or "Make that note shorter." If someone wants to estimate the cost of a party, they write the numbers down and ask, "Read it back." A clean list with no old items is easier to read, so they say, "Delete the done ones."

Aminata sat on her bed with her phone and typed to the assistant. "ok so what do i pack for the hills this weekend? i think it will drop to fifty degrees at night." The assistant made a packing list: a warm jacket, wool socks, a hat, a water bottle, a flashlight and a rain cover for the tent. "Check that the flashlight is working," it added. Aminata laughed. "Good idea. I also want to jump in the lake if it's not too cold." The assistant put a swimsuit and a towel on the list, and a note to ask the camp if swimming was allowed. Aminata ticked each item as she packed her bag. Then she texted her friends a photo of the list.

Thiago was a driver, and his shift started before the sun came up. He stood in the kitchen with a mug and made a face. "This coffee is too weak for this morning," he said, rubbing his eyes. The assistant understood he wanted it stronger. It told the coffee machine to make the next cup with extra beans and less water. Thiago opened the sugar jar and spooned in a little. "No need to rush," said the assistant, "it takes two minutes." He waited, patient now that he could smell it. The new cup was dark and rich. Thiago took a long sip, smiled, and said, "Now I can drive." Then he picked up his keys and went out to his truck.

Andre closed his laptop and then opened it again, because the kids were making noise. "Create a new folder on the computer called Trip," he told the assistant. Then his daughter waved a paper at him. "Wait, no. Call it Plane tickets instead," he said. The assistant renamed the folder. "Put the three files from my downloads in it," he added. It moved the files and told him the folder now held three items. Andre checked the screen and nodded. The battery was low, so he asked the assistant to dim the screen. When the folder was closed, he plugged in the charger and went to make the kids lunch.

name: gift_idea_finder
does: Suggests presents for a person based on what they like and how much you want to spend, and takes the pain out of last-minute shopping.
inputs: the person's age, what they enjoy, your budget, and where you are, so the shops are near you
people say:
- What should I get my brother for his birthday?
- I need a present for my teacher, nothing expensive
- Any ideas for a ten year old who loves space?
- I care about my aunt, so help me pick something nice
- Find me a gift I can buy today close to here
- My dad has everything, what now?

Offices and errands are the little trips that keep life going: a visit to the post office, a stop at the bank, or picking up a parcel. People plan them so they do not waste time. They look up opening hours and see how long the line is. They change plans by saying, "Finish my bank visit before noon," "Remind me to pick up the keys," or "Move the post office to tomorrow." A heavy box may mean going by car. In an office building, someone might also report a dripping faucet and say, "Tell the building manager."

Someone with high hopes of getting a parcel today, who has set an alarm for the delivery, wants the assistant to connect to the tracking and say where it is.
Parcel tracking
Where's my parcel?
Track it
Has my package left the depot yet?
When will the delivery come today?
Check the status of my order
Could you look up my parcel for me? I'm waiting at home and need to know if I should go out.

Someone wants to share a large number of cookies between people, and to hear the answer again if they missed it.
Split 48 between 6 people
48 divided by 6?
If six people share forty-eight cookies, how many does each get?
How many each if 6 share 48
Divide 48 by 6 and repeat the answer
I have 48 cookies for the six kids coming after school today, how many does each one get?
Could you work out how many each person gets? There are six people and forty-eight cookies, and they come after school today.

Someone who is angry that the milk ran out again wants it put on the shopping list on the kitchen console, so they can weigh up what else is running low.
Milk, list
Add milk
We're out of milk
Put milk on my list
Out of milk again!
Note that we need milk
Please remind me to buy milk, I keep running out.

Person: I'm going to a trade show in Prague next week. How much is two hundred in local money?
Assistant: Which money are you starting from?
Person: Dollars, sorry.
Assistant: Two hundred dollars is about four thousand six hundred crowns at today's rate.
Person: Good. I want to take half in cash and half on my card. Is that a safe mix?
Assistant: I can't say what is safe or best. I can tell you that half is about two thousand three hundred crowns each.
Person: That helps. Show me the rate again in the evening.
Assistant: Yes, I will tell you the rate tonight.

Someone wants to know how much longer the cream cake needs to bake before they pack it for the party, and the answer should be great news.
How long left on the cake?
Is my cake done yet?
I have to pack this by six, how long is left on the timer?
It smells like something is burning in the kitchen
The edges look dark, should I take it out?
It's getting late and I can't tell if the middle is cooked
Could you tell me how many minutes are left? I need to pack the cake in a box soon and I don't want it raw inside.

Someone needs to know if their parcel will come early, because they need to put the recycling out before the truck.
where is my parcel
wheres my package
wil it come early today?
is the delivery coming this morning
need to know when the courier comes
can u check my parcle
tell me if the mail is early, i need to be home

name: speaker_groups
does: Joins speakers in different rooms into one group so they play the same music, or divide them again, like the kitchen and the balcony.
inputs: which speakers to join or separate, and what to play, such as a happy song or a sad one
people say:
- Play this on every speaker in the house
- Put the balcony and kitchen together
- Music on the balcony too, please
- Stop playing in the bedroom, just the living room
- Split the speakers up again
- I want the same song everywhere

Sergei sat on a bench in the park while his twins played on the slide. One of them sneezed, and he wiped her nose. He felt nervous, because the school had said it might call. "Did the school call me?" he asked his phone. "And how many times?" The assistant said there were three missed calls and one voicemail. Sergei asked to hear the voicemail. It was the school nurse, saying the boys were fine and that practice had ended early. He let out a breath. Then he said, "Call my wife and put her on speaker, and make it twice as loud, the wind is strong." The assistant did, and soon his wife's voice came out clear. "We're at the park," he said, smiling.

Sabine was eating her cereal and texting with one hand when her throat began to hurt. It was sore and scratchy. "book me a doctor, not tomorrow morning, i have a test," she typed to the assistant. The assistant asked which doctor she usually saw. "Dr. Weber, the one near school." It looked up the opening hours and said the clinic closed at five today. There was a spot at four. "I don't want to miss math class either," Sabine added. The assistant checked her calendar and saw math ended at three, so four would work. It booked the visit and sent a reminder for half past three. Sabine put down her spoon, drank some water, and went to get her bag.
